theme: Disobedience; the flight to Egypt; Baruch’s consolation
readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 43:1-45:5. The leaders refuse God’s answer and flee to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them. Then Jeremiah faces the people’s idolatry in Egypt, and a short word is given to Baruch, his scribe. Read chapter 45 carefully.
settingTheScene: After God’s answer in chapter 42, the leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying and carry off the whole remnant to Egypt. In Tahpanhes, a border town, they settle among other Judean refugees. Even there, they take up the worship of the Queen of Heaven. The prophet’s last recorded sermons are directed at their stubbornness. Chapter 45 is a gentle word to Baruch, who had grown discouraged.
observation: “You are telling a lie. The LORD our God did not send you to say, Do not go to Egypt to live there” (43:2).
“So Johanan… and all the people did not obey the voice of the LORD” (43:4).
“Take some large stones and hide them in the mortar… in front of Pharaoh’s palace in Tahpanhes” (43:9).
“Why do you provoke me to anger with the work of your hands, making offerings to other gods in the land of Egypt?” (44:8).
“We will not listen to you… we will do everything that we have vowed, make offerings to the queen of heaven” (44:16-17).
“For then we had plenty of bread, and prospered, and saw no disaster” (44:17).
“Behold, I am watching over them for disaster and not for good” (44:27).

“And do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not, for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all flesh… but I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go” (45:5).
interpretation:
The people’s refusal is blunt. Having asked for God’s word and promised to obey, they now call Jeremiah a liar. The sin of unbelief is compounded by the sin of disobedience. They go to Egypt, the land God had delivered them from. It is a reversal of the exodus. The prophet is taken with them, and even there he continues to speak.

God’s word comes in the form of a sign: Jeremiah buries stones in the pavement in front of Pharaoh’s palace and says that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne over them. The refuge they chose will not hold.

In chapter 44, the people in Egypt are defiant. When Jeremiah reproaches them for their idolatry, they give a revealing response. They claim that when they worshiped the Queen of Heaven, they had food and no disaster. It was only when they stopped, in Josiah’s reform, that trouble came. This is a classic example of misreading history. They say that the gods worked and the LORD did not. They are reading their own lives with no reference to God’s word. They refuse to repent and vow to continue.

Against this, chapter 45 is a short, tender word to Baruch. He had been in the thick of the struggle with Jeremiah, writing the scrolls and being threatened. He is weary and says, “Woe is me! For the LORD has added sorrow to my pain.” God’s reply is gentle but firm: “Do you seek great things for yourself? Seek them not.” This is not a time for personal ambition. Yet there is a promise: your life will be spared. Baruch’s life is a quiet example of faithful service in a time of collapse.
connection: Luke 6:46-49 contrasts the person who hears and does not act with the one who builds on rock. Matthew 6:33 says to seek first the kingdom of God, which echoes “seek not great things.” Luke 9:23-25 says that whoever would save his life will lose it. Philippians 2:3-4 calls us to count others more significant than ourselves. Hebrews 3:12-13 warns against an evil, unbelieving heart.
application:
Ask whether you ever read your life only through your own experience and not through God’s word.

Think about whether you are “seeking great things” for yourself. What would it mean to be content with faithful, hidden service?

Encourage someone who is faithfully serving in a quiet role.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from a hard heart that calls his word a lie.
Ask him to teach you to read your life through his word.
